“Alright O.K. You Win” that was on there?

items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I considered myself a master at writing blues, especially Basie-type blues, so writing for Joe Williams was easy.

ctx.x: Talk a bit about writing for Joe [Williams], your contributions in that area and what particular challenge that might have been or what approach you felt he needed.

Writing for Joe was pretty much a snap, because he was better known as a blues singer than anything else. I considered myself a master at writing blues, especially Basie-type blues, so writing for Joe Williams was easy. The challenge was to couch his voice in phrases and passages that would just enhance his vocal statements.
Can you give me an example of how you did that, or where you think that was particularly successful?

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: Well you certainly had a powerhouse band there for those years, plus with Joe Williams on board

ctx.x: Well the professionalism in this particular orchestra didn’t allow for that kind of attitude on a large scale. And we loved Sinatra, we loved Billy Eckstine, we loved Sarah Vaughan and we loved Tony Bennett, and there just was no feeling of that kind. Whenever we knew we were going to work with them we said well we’re going to have some fun now. Some others, who shall remain nameless, we didn’t have as much fun with because some of them didn’t have the quality arrangements that we would like to play, and some of…
Well you certainly had a powerhouse band there for those years, plus with Joe Williams on board, and a great time. Fortunately you recorded a lot so it’s documented.
Yes. It definitely is documented, especially in the Mosaic series of live recordings between 1959 and ‘62. That is Count Basie, the New Testament Count Basie.
